references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus uses the same image of the beam and the speck in the eye, and calls the one who judges a hypocrite (ὑποκριτά) who must first remove the beam from his own eye.
Paul warns against judging others, because the one who judges does the same himself – the same principle Jesus teaches about seeing the speck in another's eye while overlooking the beam in one's own.
Paul asks rhetorically: you who teach others, do you not teach yourself? The one who admonishes others without seeing their own sin resembles the hypocrite Jesus mentions.
The prophet Nathan uses a parable to expose David's sin. David judged the rich man without seeing his own guilt – an example of seeing the speck in another's eye but not the beam in one's own.
The one who speaks first in a case seems to be right – a proverb that reminds us of the tendency to judge others without self-examination.

Paul urges believers to restore a brother caught in sin with gentleness, and to watch themselves so they are not tempted – the same spirit as Jesus' words about first removing the beam from one's own eye.

James warns against slandering and judging one's brother, because the one who judges their brother sets themselves up as judge over the law – a warning against the hypocritical attitude Jesus rebukes.
Jesus says, "He who is without sin among you may cast the first stone" – the same principle of examining oneself before judging others.
Jesus calls the scribes and Pharisees hypocrites (ὑποκριταί). The use of the word 'hypocrite' in Luke 6:42 connects to Jesus' repeated condemnation of hypocrisy.
